newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica plays down report on Manuel replacement.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica plays down report on Manuel replacement.

text.p: A South African presidential spokesman on Friday played down a newspaper report that Finance Minister Trevor Manuel would be replaced in a major cabinet reshuffle in the coming weeks, but did not deny that changes might be in the works.

Spokesman Parks Mankahlana, an aide to President Nelson Mandela, was commenting on a front-page report in the Cape Times newspaper, which said Manuel, South Africa's first black finance minister, would likely be replaced by current Trade and industry Minister Alec Erwin, a white.
"It's sheer speculation at this stage," the spokesman told Reuters.
The Cape Times said at least four cabinet changes would be announced when Mandela opened parliament in Cape Town in early February.

Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo and Defence Minister Joe Modise would retire for reasons of age and ill health and Finance and Trade and Industry would get new ministers in what the paper called the most significant reshuffle since Mandela's government took office nearly three years ago.
The Cape Town daily quoted "top sources" in Mandela's ruling African National Congress for its report, which hardened rumours circulating recently in political circles and financial markets.
One ANC source who spoke to Reuters on condition on anonymity said: "There is a perception that Manuel has to go. Not that he has been a disaster but he's not seen as quite up to the job."

Manuel assumed South Africa's most daunting portfolio last April, when Chris Liebenberg quit the government. He took the helm as South Africa's rand currency was falling steeply, but despite efforts to gain the confidence of the markets, the slide could not be arrested and the rand ended up losing 30 percent of its value against the dollar in 1996.
The ANC source said Manuel could be moved into the foreign affairs portfolio, where Nzo has signally failed to impress critics but where Manuel's international connections could pay off.

Asked recently about rumours that he would soon be moved to the foreign ministry, Manuel was quoted by the Financial Mail magazine as saying: "Ach no man. Over here I can kick ass. Over there I would have to kiss it."

Despite his radical political background -- a trade union organiser who remains a member of the South African Communist Party, which is part of Mandela's governing alliance -- trade minister Alec Erwin "has gained the confidence of the business community", the ANC source told Reuters.

The Cape Times said Erwin was "well-liked in business circles and is credited with steering government economic policies on a conservative course, favouring limited government spending, privatisation initiatives and a cut-back in public sector jobs".
Erwin presided over a major United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD) conference in April last year, the first U.N. conference to be hosted by South Africa.
